newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavarian premier wants strict rules in euro club.
newsitem.headline: Bavarian premier wants strict rules in euro club.

text.p: Bavarian premier Edmund Stoiber, one of Germany's staunchest advocates of a rock-hard single European currency, said on Thursday monetary union should be an elite club whose members are committed.

Stoiber said that because Germany's European partners had not accepted widespread automatic fines for members of the single currency who did not stick to strict financial targets, Bonn had to be very vigilant in scrutinising potential members.
"We must take care that only countries who are committed to a culture of stability enter the euro-club," he told the news magazine Der Spiegel.

"If members are only allowed into a club wearing ties, you have to make sure they all keep them on inside," said Stoiber, a member of Finance Minister Theo Waigel's conservative Christian Social Union (CSU) party.

Stoiber, often seen as a rival to Waigel and a possible successor to German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said there could be no concessions for countries who tried but failed to meet the Maastricht criteria for economic and monetary union (EMU), due to begin in 1999.
"We can't accept a country if it doesn't meet the criteria, even if it's still trying very hard. It's an economic matter, not a political one," he said.

German opinion formers doubt southern European countries such as Italy and Spain would manage their economies soundly if they were accepted as founder members of a single currency. Their membership is seen as potentially damaging to EMU.
Stoiber also cautioned that a weak European currency would shake the public's faith in mainstream politicians, as life insurance and savings would effectively be devalued.
"In the year 2003 or 2004, a German Le Pen or a German Joerg Haider could exploit that," he said, referring to the populist hard-right leaders in France and Austria.
